guide.title: Fisherman's Wharf, San Francisco: Pier 39, the sea lions, Aquatic Park and Ghirardelli Square
guide.intro: Fisherman's Wharf is the strip of working and former working waterfront on San Francisco's northern bay shore, running from Pier 39 west to Aquatic Park. Most of what a visitor comes for is packed into about a mile of it: a colony of California sea lions that has hauled out at Pier 39 since 1989, a Second World War submarine at Pier 45 with a hall of coin-operated arcade machines in the shed beside it, a chocolate factory converted into a block of shops in 1964, and a curved public beach built by the Works Progress Administration. Two cable car lines end here, each on its own turntable. One large caveat applies at the moment: Hyde Street Pier is closed while it is rebuilt, and the five museum ships that used to lie against it have been moved out of the city.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Two of the three cable car lines end at the wharf. SFMTA gives the Powell-Hyde terminus at Hyde and Beach Streets, on the grass of Victorian Park, and the Powell-Mason terminus at Bay and Taylor Streets; both lines start at Powell and Market. Advance purchase through MuniMobile or a Clipper card is required at Powell and Market, at Bay and Taylor, and at Hyde and Beach between 08.00 and 20.00 daily. SFMTA publishes no operating hours for the lines, so none are given here.

Steer by street addresses rather than by the water, because the piers are numbered along the shore rather than in a line you can follow. Pier 39 gives its own address as Beach Street and The Embarcadero, and Aquarium of the Bay is inside it. Pier 45 holds USS Pampanito at its berth and the Musee Mecanique in Shed A. Scoma's is at 1965 Al Scoma Way, on Pier 47. The SkyStar Wheel stands at 2860 Taylor Street and Pompei's Grotto at 340 Jefferson Street. Ghirardelli Square is at 900 North Point Street; the Argonaut Hotel and the national park's visitor center share 680 Beach Street in the old Haslett Warehouse; and the Buena Vista Cafe is at 2765 Hyde Street, on the corner of Beach Street beside the Powell-Hyde turntable.

sections.heading: The museum ships have left the pier
sections.body:
San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park was established in 1988, and its 50 acres have grown around Aquatic Park Cove. Five of its vessels are square-rigged, paddle-driven and steam-powered survivors of the Pacific coast trades: Balclutha of 1886, the ferryboat Eureka of 1890, the lumber schooner C. A. Thayer of 1895, the scow schooner Alma of 1891 and the tug Hercules of 1907. None of them is currently in San Francisco. The ships of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park are berthed at the Mare Island Coal Sheds in Vallejo while Hyde Street Pier is rebuilt. The National Park Service gives that temporary site as 860 Nimitz Avenue, Vallejo, CA 94592, and states that Hyde Street Pier is closed.

USS Pampanito is a separate case and is not affected. The submarine is operated by the San Francisco Maritime National Park Association rather than by the National Park Service, its address of record on the National Register is Fisherman's Wharf-Pier 45, and the park's closure notice does not cover it.

Three parts of the park remain open. The visitor center is in the Haslett Warehouse at 680 Beach Street; the Maritime Museum occupies the Aquatic Park Bathhouse at the foot of Polk Street; and Aquatic Park Cove, the protected water the swimming clubs use, is open. The Municipal Pier that curves out from the same shore is not: it has been closed to the public since 2022.

sections.heading: Opening hours along the waterfront
sections.body:
Pier 39 publishes its hours by category rather than as one line: retail 10.00 to 21.00, full-service restaurants 11.00 to 22.00, fast food 10.00 to 21.00, attractions 10.00 to 21.00, and outdoor vendor carts and kiosks 11.00 to 20.00. Aquarium of the Bay, inside it, opens Monday to Sunday from 10.00 to 17.00. The SkyStar Wheel on Taylor Street opens daily from 10.00 to 22.00.

For food, Scoma's opens Monday to Thursday and Sunday from 12.00 to 21.30 and Friday and Saturday from 12.00 to 22.00, with the bar from 11.30 daily, and closes on Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. The Buena Vista Cafe opens Monday to Thursday 10.00 to 23.00, Friday and Saturday 9.00 to 24.00 and Sunday 9.00 to 23.00, with the kitchen closing at 21.30. Pompei's Grotto opens daily at 11.00 and serves lunch and dinner 363 days a year, closing on Christmas Eve night and Christmas Day; lunch runs until 16.00 and dinner is served all day. At Boudin, breakfast is served at Bakers Hall from 8.00 to 11.00, and no full opening hours are published, so none are given here.

Two things a visitor expects to find scheduled are not. The Musee Mecanique publishes neither hours nor an admission price, and no source states either, so none are given here; the same is true of the two cable car turntables. The Dolphin Club at Aquatic Park is a members' club open to its own members seven days a week from 5.00 to 22.00, with public day use on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays only: 9.00 to 17.00 from 1 November to 30 April, and 8.00 to 17.00 from 1 May to 31 October.

faq.question: Can you see the historic ships at Hyde Street Pier?
faq.answer: Not at the moment. The ships of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park are berthed at the Mare Island Coal Sheds in Vallejo while Hyde Street Pier is rebuilt. The National Park Service gives that address as 860 Nimitz Avenue, Vallejo, CA 94592, and states that the pier itself is closed. USS Pampanito is the exception: it lies at Pier 45, it is run by the San Francisco Maritime National Park Association rather than by the National Park Service, and the park's closure notice does not cover it. The park's visitor center in the Haslett Warehouse, the Maritime Museum in the Aquatic Park Bathhouse and Aquatic Park Cove are all open.

faq.question: Where are the sea lions, and when did they arrive?
faq.answer: A colony of California sea lions began hauling out at Pier 39 in September 1989 and the animals are still there. No source states which of the pier's docks they use, so none is given here. Pier 39 gives its own address as Beach Street and The Embarcadero, and its attractions open from 10.00 to 21.00.

faq.question: Which cable cars come to the wharf, and where do they turn around?
faq.answer: The Powell-Hyde line ends at a turntable at Hyde and Beach Streets, standing in Victorian Park, and the Powell-Mason line ends at a turntable at Bay and Taylor Streets. SFMTA states that both lines start at Powell and Market, and that advance purchase through MuniMobile or a Clipper card is required at Powell and Market, at Bay and Taylor, and at Hyde and Beach between 08.00 and 20.00 daily. SFMTA publishes no operating hours for the lines, so none are given here.

faq.question: What is Aquatic Park?
faq.answer: A curved public beach and lagoon with a Streamline Moderne bathhouse behind it, built by the Works Progress Administration between 1936 and 1939. The bathhouse now holds the Maritime Museum. The Aquatic Park Historic District was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 26 January 1984, reference number 84001183, and was designated a National Historic Landmark district on 28 May 1987; California Historical Landmark No. 236, designated in 1936, marks the entrance of the San Carlos into San Francisco Bay at this place. The register describes the district as bounded by Van Ness Avenue, Hyde and Polk Streets, and its contributing elements are the beach, the bathhouse, the horseshoe-shaped Municipal Pier, restrooms, a concessions stand, the stadia and two speaker towers.

faq.question: Which buildings at the wharf carry designations?
faq.answer: Ghirardelli Square, at 900 North Point Street, is San Francisco Landmark No. 30, designated in 1970, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 29 April 1982 as Pioneer Woolen Mills and D. Ghirardelli Company, reference number 82002249. The Haslett Warehouse at 680 Beach Street, which now holds the Argonaut Hotel and the national park's visitor center, is San Francisco Landmark No. 59, designated in 1974, and was listed on the National Register on 28 March 1975, reference number 75000172. Neither Pier 39 nor Pier 43, Pier 45 or the Musee Mecanique appears on the Article 10 list.

photos.title: Ghirardelli Square from North Point Street
photos.description: The brick buildings of Ghirardelli Square at 900 North Point Street, with the rooftop Ghirardelli sign above them, seen from street level in daylight.
photos.author: The wub

places.name: Pier 39
places.address: Beach Street and The Embarcadero, San Francisco, CA 94133
places.summary: A two-level pier of shops, restaurants and attractions built out over the bay at the foot of Beach Street. Its own site gives retail hours of 10.00 to 21.00, full-service restaurants 11.00 to 22.00, fast food 10.00 to 21.00, attractions 10.00 to 21.00, and outdoor vendor carts and kiosks 11.00 to 20.00. Aquarium of the Bay is inside it, and the sea lion colony lies against its docks.
places.history: Pier 39 was developed by Warren Simmons and opened on 4 October 1978.

places.name: The Pier 39 sea lions
places.summary: A colony of California sea lions began hauling out at Pier 39 in September 1989, and the animals have been on the pier's floating docks since. No source states which dock they use, so none is given here. They are wild animals on public water, free to look at, and they come and go with the fish.
places.history: No source states a further history of the colony.

places.name: Aquarium of the Bay
places.address: Pier 39, The Embarcadero at Beach Street, San Francisco, CA 94133
places.summary: A non-profit aquarium on Pier 39 devoted to the animals of San Francisco Bay, open Monday to Sunday from 10.00 to 17.00. Its galleries are Discover the Bay, Go with the Flow, Under the Bay and Touch the Bay. Under the Bay runs two 300-foot tunnels holding more than 200 species, and the aquarium keeps river otters.
places.history: No source states an institutional history of the aquarium.

places.name: Pier 45
places.summary: A fish-handling pier with long working sheds. USS Pampanito is berthed against it and the Musee Mecanique occupies Shed A. It is not on the Article 10 list of San Francisco landmarks.
places.history: No source states a construction date for the pier.

places.name: USS Pampanito
places.summary: A Balao-class diesel-electric submarine open to visitors at Pier 45, operated by the San Francisco Maritime National Park Association. She is not a National Park Service vessel, so the closure of Hyde Street Pier and the move of the park's fleet to Vallejo do not affect her.
places.history: Pampanito was built at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in Kittery, Maine, launched on 12 July 1943 and commissioned on 6 November 1943. She has been a museum ship in San Francisco since 21 November 1975. She was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 14 January 1986, reference number 86000089, and is a National Historic Landmark.

places.name: Musee Mecanique
places.summary: A working collection of coin-operated machines in Shed A on Pier 45: music boxes, fortune tellers, Mutoscopes, player pianos, peep shows, photo booths, dioramas and pinball. More than 300 machines are held and about 200 are on display at a time. No source states its opening hours or its admission price, so none are given here.
places.history: The collection was assembled by Ed Zelinsky and is directed by his son, Dan Zelinsky. Among the machines are a Praxinoscope built in 1884, a steam-powered motorcycle built in Sacramento in 1912, the Royal Court diorama shown at the Panama-Pacific International Exposition, and Laffing Sal, a six-foot laughing automaton. The collection stood at Playland from 1928 to 1972 and then in the basement of the Cliff House.

places.name: Pier 43 Ferry Arch
places.summary: A steel arch and headhouse standing on the shore at Pier 43. The headhouse was a decorated hoisting tower, built to lift rail cars on and off the ferries that carried freight across the bay.
places.history: The arch opened in 1914, built to serve the Belt Railroad. The wooden pier behind it was replaced in 1996. The headhouse was damaged by fire in 1998 and rehabilitated between 2002 and 2003 to the Secretary of the Interior's Standards.

places.name: SkyStar Wheel
places.summary: A 150-foot observation wheel at 2860 Taylor Street, open daily from 10.00 to 22.00. Its gondolas are enclosed and climate-controlled, which matters on a waterfront where the summer afternoon wind is cold.
places.history: The SkyStar Wheel began operating at Fisherman's Wharf on 13 November 2023.

places.name: Ripley's Believe It or Not! San Francisco
places.summary: An oddities museum on Jefferson Street, part of the Ripley's chain. No source states its street number or its opening hours, so neither is given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the San Francisco branch.

places.name: San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park
places.summary: The national park that holds Hyde Street Pier, the Maritime Museum in the Aquatic Park Bathhouse, the visitor center in the Haslett Warehouse, Aquatic Park Cove and a fleet of historic ships. San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park was established in 1988, and its 50 acres have grown around Aquatic Park Cove. The ships of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park are berthed at the Mare Island Coal Sheds in Vallejo while Hyde Street Pier is rebuilt.
places.history: The fleet is Balclutha, a square-rigger of 1886; the ferryboat Eureka of 1890; the lumber schooner C. A. Thayer of 1895; the scow schooner Alma of 1891; and the steam tug Hercules of 1907. Each is separately listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and each address of record is in San Francisco County.

places.name: Hyde Street Pier
places.summary: The pier at 2905 Hyde Street, part of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park and, until recently, the berth of its fleet. It is closed while it is rebuilt. The ships of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park are berthed at the Mare Island Coal Sheds in Vallejo while Hyde Street Pier is rebuilt.
places.history: Before the Golden Gate and Bay Bridges opened, Hyde Street Pier was an automobile-ferry terminal, carrying US 101 to Sausalito and US 40 to Berkeley. The ferries were run by the Golden Gate Ferry Company, which merged with Southern Pacific's auto-ferry system in early 1929; from 1 May 1929 the service was taken over by Southern Pacific-Golden Gate Ferries, Ltd.

places.name: Balclutha
places.summary: A three-masted square-rigged ship of 1886, part of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park. The ships of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park are berthed at the Mare Island Coal Sheds in Vallejo while Hyde Street Pier is rebuilt.
places.history: Balclutha was built in 1886 by Charles Connell & Co. Ltd near Glasgow: 256.50 feet in length, 38.65 feet in beam, 22.75 feet depth of hold, 1,689.30 gross tons. She carried grain between California and Europe from 1887 to 1899, Pacific lumber under Hawaiian registry from 1899 to 1902, and Alaska salmon as Star of Alaska from 1902 to 1930. From 1933 to 1954 she worked as a film ship under the name Pacific Queen. She was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 7 November 1976, reference number 76000178, and is a National Historic Landmark.

places.name: Eureka
places.summary: A side-wheel paddle steamboat of 1890, part of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park. The ships of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park are berthed at the Mare Island Coal Sheds in Vallejo while Hyde Street Pier is rebuilt.
places.history: She was built in 1890 by John Dickie at Tiburon and first named Ukiah: 299.5 feet overall, 78 feet extreme width, 2,420 gross tons. She carried railway cars and passengers between Sausalito and San Francisco, was rebuilt in 1923 and renamed Eureka, and ran until 1957. California State Parks took her in 1963 and the National Park Service in 1977. She was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 24 April 1973, reference number 73000229, and is a National Historic Landmark.

places.name: C. A. Thayer
places.summary: A three-masted bald-headed lumber schooner of 1895, part of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park. The ships of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park are berthed at the Mare Island Coal Sheds in Vallejo while Hyde Street Pier is rebuilt.
places.history: She was built in 1895 by Hans D. Bendixsen near Humboldt Bay: 219 feet in full length, 156 feet on deck, 11.38 feet depth of hold, 453 gross tons, with a 105-foot mainmast. She carried lumber from Grays Harbor to San Francisco from 1895 to 1912, with voyages to Mexico, Hawaii and Fiji; salmon out of Bristol Bay from 1912 to 1924; and cod from the Bering Sea from 1925 to 1950. From 1954 to 1957 she stood beside a road in Hood Canal as a pirate ship, and she has been a museum ship since 1963. She was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 13 November 1966, reference number 66000229, and is a National Historic Landmark.

places.name: Alma
places.summary: A scow schooner of 1891, flat-bottomed and built for the shallow water of the bay and its rivers, and part of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park. The ships of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park are berthed at the Mare Island Coal Sheds in Vallejo while Hyde Street Pier is rebuilt.
places.history: She was built in 1891 by Fred Siemer: 80 feet overall, 59 feet on the register, 22.6 feet in beam, 4 feet depth, 41.76 gross tons, with a 67-foot foremast. She carried hay and lumber under sail; her masts came out in 1918 and she worked as a towed salt barge; from 1926 she hauled oyster shell to Petaluma, 110 to 125 tons a week, until 1957. California bought her in 1959, restoration began in 1964, and the National Park Service took her in 1978. She was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 10 October 1975, reference number 75000179, and is a National Historic Landmark.

places.name: Hercules
places.summary: An ocean-going steam tug of 1907, riveted steel, still carrying her original triple-expansion steam engine, and part of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park. The ships of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park are berthed at the Mare Island Coal Sheds in Vallejo while Hyde Street Pier is rebuilt.
places.history: She was built in 1907 by John H. Dialogue and Son of Camden, New Jersey, for the Red Stack fleet of the Shipowners' and Merchants' Tugboat Company: 151 feet long, 26 feet in beam, 409 gross tons. She towed her sister Goliah around South America to San Francisco, and afterwards towed sailing vessels, log rafts and barges, among them a caisson for the Pearl Harbor dry dock and another for the Panama Canal works. She finished on Western Pacific Railroad car barges until 1962. She was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1975, reference number 75000225, and is a National Historic Landmark.

places.name: San Francisco Maritime Museum, Aquatic Park Bathhouse
places.summary: The bathhouse at the foot of Polk Street, standing behind the Aquatic Park beach and now holding the maritime museum. The National Park Service describes it as Streamline Moderne, defined by sweeping lines, curved facades, stainless steel railings and porthole windows, its design evoking a ship at port. It is a contributing building of the Aquatic Park Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1984, reference number 84001183.
places.history: William Mooser III designed the building under the supervision of his father, William Mooser II. It was built by the Works Progress Administration between 1936 and 1939 at a cost of $1.5 million, and the dedication ceremony on 22 January 1939 drew a crowd of 10,000.

places.name: San Francisco Maritime Park Visitor Center
places.summary: The visitor center of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park, inside the Haslett Warehouse at 680 Beach Street, sharing the building with the Argonaut Hotel. The National Park Service gives it as open. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Its building is the Haslett Warehouse, San Francisco Landmark No. 59, designated in 1974, and listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1975, reference number 75000172.

places.name: Aquatic Park Historic District
places.summary: The Works Progress Administration complex around Aquatic Park Cove: a curved beach and lagoon, the bathhouse that now holds the Maritime Museum, the horseshoe-shaped Municipal Pier, restrooms, a concessions stand, the stadia and two speaker towers. The National Register describes the district as bounded by Van Ness Avenue, Hyde and Polk Streets.
places.history: The Aquatic Park Historic District was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 26 January 1984, reference number 84001183, and was designated a National Historic Landmark district on 28 May 1987. California Historical Landmark No. 236, designated in 1936, marks the entrance of the San Carlos into San Francisco Bay at this place. The buildings of the district were put up between 1936 and 1939.

places.name: Aquatic Park Cove
places.summary: A protected area of San Francisco Bay, sheltered from the shipping channel, and the water around which the 50 acres of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park have grown. It is open, and it is where the swimming clubs on its shore swim.
places.history: No source states a separate history of the cove.

places.name: Municipal Pier
places.summary: The horseshoe-shaped pier curving out into the bay from the western side of Aquatic Park. It is a contributing element of the Aquatic Park Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1984, reference number 84001183. It has been closed to the public since 2022.
places.history: No source states a construction date or a length for the pier, so neither is given here.

places.name: Victorian Park
places.summary: A grassy area on Beach Street at Hyde Street, inside the Aquatic Park Historic District, which is listed on the National Register of Historic Places under reference number 84001183. The Powell-Hyde cable car turntable stands in it, so the park doubles as the queue for the ride back up the hill.
places.history: No source states a construction date for the park, so none is given here.

places.name: Dolphin Club
places.summary: A volunteer-led swimming and rowing club at Aquatic Park, with a membership of more than 1,800 and a boathouse at Lake Merced. Members use it seven days a week from 5.00 to 22.00. Public day use runs on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays: 9.00 to 17.00 from 1 November to 30 April, and 8.00 to 17.00 from 1 May to 31 October. Sources give conflicting street numbers for the clubhouse, so none is given here.
places.history: No source states a history of the club.

places.name: Ghirardelli Square
places.address: 900 North Point Street, San Francisco, CA
places.summary: A chocolate factory turned into a block of shops and restaurants around open courtyards, at 900 North Point Street. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 30, designated in 1970, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 29 April 1982 as Pioneer Woolen Mills and D. Ghirardelli Company, reference number 82002249.
places.history: Domenico Ghirardelli bought the whole city block in 1893 to make it the headquarters of the Ghirardelli Chocolate Company. In the early 1960s the Golden Grain Macaroni Company bought the business, moved the headquarters to San Leandro and put the block up for sale. William M. Roth and his mother, Lurline Matson Roth, bought the land in 1962; they hired the landscape architect Lawrence Halprin and the architects Wurster, Bernardi & Emmons, and the converted square opened in 1964. Benjamin Thompson and Associates reworked the lower floor of the Clock Tower in 1965 for a Design Research store.

places.name: Haslett Warehouse and the Argonaut Hotel
places.summary: A brick and timber warehouse at 680 Beach Street, now a 252-room hotel that opened in August 2003, sharing the building with the visitor center of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park. The hotel gives its own frontage as 495 Jefferson Street; both addresses are the same building. It is San Francisco Landmark No. 59, designated in 1974, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on 28 March 1975, reference number 75000172.
places.history: It was built between 1907 and 1909 to a design by William S. Mooser Jr. for the California Fruit Canners Association, and stored Central Valley produce canned east of the warehouse. In 1916 the association merged into California Packing, which sold under the Del Monte label. The National Park Service leased the roughly 198,000 square feet to Kimpton in 2002 on a 57-year term, and the building remains part of the park.

places.name: Boudin Bakery
places.summary: The Boudin flagship on Jefferson Street, built around a working sourdough bakery that visitors watch through a 30-foot observation window with a two-way intercom to the bakers. Bakers Hall holds the marketplace, the cafe and the espresso bar; Bistro Boudin is a full-service waterfront restaurant. Breakfast is served at Bakers Hall from 8.00 to 11.00, and no source states full opening hours, so none are given here. No source settles its street number either.
places.history: No source states a history of the building.

places.name: Buena Vista Cafe
places.summary: A bar and cafe at 2765 Hyde Street, on the corner of Beach Street, facing the Powell-Hyde cable car turntable. Monday to Thursday 10.00 to 23.00, Friday and Saturday 9.00 to 24.00, Sunday 9.00 to 23.00. The kitchen closes at 21.30.
places.history: No source states a history of the cafe.

places.name: Scoma's
places.address: 1965 Al Scoma Way, San Francisco, CA 94133
places.summary: A seafood restaurant at 1965 Al Scoma Way, on Pier 47. It sits on a working pier. Monday to Thursday and Sunday 12.00 to 21.30; Friday and Saturday 12.00 to 22.00; the bar opens at 11.30 daily. It closes on Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day.
places.history: No source states a history of the restaurant.

places.name: Pompei's Grotto
places.summary: A family restaurant at 340 Jefferson Street, open daily at 11.00. Its own site gives lunch and dinner 363 days a year, closing on Christmas Eve night and Christmas Day; dinner is served all day and lunch runs until 16.00.
places.history: No source states a history of the restaurant.

places.name: Powell-Hyde cable car turntable
places.summary: The turntable at Hyde and Beach Streets where the Powell-Hyde cable car line ends, standing in Victorian Park. SFMTA states that the line starts at Powell and Market, and that advance purchase through MuniMobile or a Clipper card is required at Powell and Market, at Bay and Taylor, and at Hyde and Beach between 08.00 and 20.00 daily. No operating hours are published for the line, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a construction date for the turntable.

places.name: Powell-Mason cable car turntable
places.summary: The turntable at Bay and Taylor Streets where the Powell-Mason cable car line ends. SFMTA states that the line starts at Powell and Market, and that advance purchase through MuniMobile or a Clipper card is required at Powell and Market, at Bay and Taylor, and at Hyde and Beach between 08.00 and 20.00 daily. No operating hours are published for the line, so none are given here.
places.history: No source states a construction date for the turntable.

entries.name: Pier 39
entries.note: Developed by Warren Simmons and opened on 4 October 1978; its shops run 10.00 to 21.00 and its full-service restaurants 11.00 to 22.00.

entries.name: The Pier 39 sea lions
entries.note: A colony of California sea lions began hauling out at Pier 39 in September 1989 and has been on the floating docks since.

entries.name: USS Pampanito
entries.note: A Balao-class submarine launched on 12 July 1943, a museum ship at Pier 45 since 21 November 1975, and listed on the National Register of Historic Places under reference number 86000089.

entries.name: Musee Mecanique
entries.note: More than 300 coin-operated machines in Shed A on Pier 45, including an 1884 Praxinoscope and Laffing Sal, a six-foot laughing automaton.

entries.name: Pier 43 Ferry Arch
entries.note: A hoisting tower of 1914, built to lift rail cars on and off ferries for the Belt Railroad, and rehabilitated in 2002 and 2003 after a fire.

entries.name: Ghirardelli Square
entries.note: The chocolate works Domenico Ghirardelli assembled from 1893, converted by Lawrence Halprin and Wurster, Bernardi & Emmons and opened as a shopping square in 1964. San Francisco Landmark No. 30.

entries.name: San Francisco Maritime Museum
entries.note: The Streamline Moderne bathhouse built by the Works Progress Administration between 1936 and 1939 and dedicated on 22 January 1939 before a crowd of 10,000.

entries.name: Aquatic Park Historic District
entries.note: Beach, lagoon, bathhouse, stadia and speaker towers between Van Ness Avenue, Hyde and Polk Streets, listed on the National Register of Historic Places under reference number 84001183.

entries.name: Victorian Park
entries.note: The grass on Beach Street at Hyde Street where the Powell-Hyde cable car turns around.

entries.name: Aquatic Park Cove
entries.note: The sheltered water the national park's 50 acres have grown around, and where the clubs on its shore swim.

entries.name: The Argonaut Hotel
entries.note: 252 rooms in the Haslett Warehouse of 1907 to 1909, opened as a hotel in August 2003 and sharing the building with the national park's visitor center.

entries.name: Scoma's
entries.note: A seafood house at 1965 Al Scoma Way on Pier 47, open from 12.00 daily and with the bar from 11.30.

entries.name: Buena Vista Cafe
entries.note: A bar at 2765 Hyde Street facing the cable car turntable, open from 10.00 on weekdays and from 9.00 at weekends, with the kitchen closing at 21.30.

entries.name: Hyde Street Pier
entries.note: The pier is closed while it is rebuilt, and the ships of San Francisco Maritime National Historical Park are berthed at the Mare Island Coal Sheds in Vallejo.

links.note: The hill immediately behind Aquatic Park, reached by the Powell-Hyde cable car: Lombard Street's crooked block, Macondray Lane and Ina Coolbrith Park.
The neighbour east and uphill of Pier 39: Washington Square, City Lights Booksellers, Coit Tower and the Telegraph Hill steps.
West along the same shore, holding Fort Mason, the Palace of Fine Arts, Marina Green and the Wave Organ.
Where the two cable car lines that end at the wharf are wound: the Cable Car Museum on Mason Street, with Grace Cathedral and Huntington Park above.
